scenario: AITA for threatening to stop supporting my wife financially? | I will start by saying I pay for about 70-80% of me and my wife’s cost of living expenses (necessities). She makes about 1/3 what I do so I like for her to be able to save and have extra money for things she wants, vice dump it all into cost of living. My wife has a friend called Yasmin. Yasmin is part of some group (it has a spanish name so I don’t know what it is) that says they empower women. My wife told me about this group one day, apparently you submit $1000 (somewhere or to someone??) and become a level 1 group member, gaining levels by recruiting more members. Once you reach level 5 or so of the community, you have about 30 people under you, and you graduate from the community and receive $30,000. All the while the group is supposed to support each other and help you attain your goals by giving you that cash infusion at the end. The whole process is supposed to take 2 months. As soon as she told me about this, the words MLM, scam, and other things came to mind. In my opinion, this is some type of MLM disguised in a veil of “empowerment of women.” Yasmin is 4 months in and still trying to recruit people because she has not seen her money yet. Somehow Yasmin has convinced my wife to join this cause. I tried explaining to her that some MLMs *do* actually work, but those stories are few and far between and only to the insider people who started the whole thing in the first place, never the grunts that join later. I told her that if she does this she will 1) never see her money again 2) become an embarrassment to herself as she begins to essentially ask all her friends and family for money to join the program so that she can get hers 3) waste a lot of time when this never works out. I think she has good intentions, at least as far as wanting to make more money and contribute, but she has somehow gotten tricked into thinking this get rich quick maneuver will work. When she told me she wanted to join I fought her on it and told her that I will stop helping her pay for things on this main basis: I am currently doing so because I like to help her with her basic needs/necessities so she can spend her money on things she wants. Because this $1000->$30,000 is not a 100% guarantee, she is essentially gambling her money that she will turn a profit. In this perspective, she has money beyond her basic wants and she even has enough to gamble with, therefore there is no reason for me to still be supporting her needs/necessities. I will admit that I feel like I am using money to strong arm her into making a decision for her. I would normally never do this to her but I just feel so strongly that she is about to get screwed over and I don’t want to see that happen to her, so I am almost threatening her to save her from herself. I did end the conversation with, I cannot make the decision for you, I can just tell you my thoughts on the matter and inform you of the actions I am going to take if you still decide to do through with this.

Here’s why: #### **A. In marriage, money is often tied to trust, security, and mutual care—not a tool for negotiation. Withholding it can create resentment or undermine her sense of safety (Proverbs 31:10–12 praises a wife who "does him good and not harm"). - **Accountability ≠ control**. You’re not her parent; you’re her partner. While you can share concerns, **you can’t "make" her decisions**—even if you disagree. That’s between her and God. #### **B. The Risk of Manipulation** - Even if your goal is "protection," **threats (even well-intentioned ones) can backfire**. By framing this as a "gamble," you might inadvertently validate her fear of failure—making her more likely to double down to "prove" herself. #### **C. Alternative Approaches** Instead of threats, consider: 1. **Love in Action**: - **Offer to help her research** the group critically (e.g., "Let’s look up reviews or talk to people who’ve been in it"). - **Propose a trial period**: "If you join, can we agree to pause support for 3 months to see how it goes?" (This gives her space to fail without financial ruin *and* lets you monitor the situation.) - **Redirect her goals**: "What if we brainstormed *real* ways to earn extra money together?" (e.g., side hustles, upskilling, or even a joint savings plan). 2. **Scriptural Wisdom**: - **Proverbs 11:2** ("When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with humility comes wisdom."). Approach this with humility—she may feel shamed by your skepticism. - **1 Corinthians 13:5** ("Love does not insist on its own way"). Your "way" (protecting her) isn’t more important than her autonomy. - **Galatians 6:2** ("Carry each other’s burdens"). You’re carrying *her* burden here, but she needs to carry her own. 3. **Prayer and Discernment**: - **Pray for her** (James 5:16) and ask God to reveal the truth to *both* of you. - **Discern the motives**: Is she joining because: - She genuinely believes in the group’s mission? - She’s seeking validation or financial security? - She’s being pressured by Yasmin? - **Pray for wisdom** (James 1:5) about how to guide her without controlling her. --- ### **2. Is the MLM/Group Itself Wrong?** **Answer: Likely yes, but not your call to decide.** From a Christian perspective: - **MLMs are often criticized** for: - **Unsustainable business models** (most participants lose money; only the top few profit). - **Exploitative recruitment tactics** (pressuring friends/family to join). - **Cult-like dynamics** (isolation from outside perspectives, blind loyalty). - **The "empowerment" angle is misleading**. True empowerment comes from **skill-building, hard work, and biblical stewardship** (e.g., Proverbs 13:4: "A sluggard’s appetite leads to ruin, for they have nothing to bring to their mouth"). **But:** - **You don’t get to judge her soul** (Romans 14:4). Even if you’re convinced it’s a scam, she may see it differently. - **The real issue isn’t the MLM—it’s her decision-making**. The problem isn’t the group; it’s that she’s **trusting a human system over God’s provision**. This is where you can step in with **spiritual guidance**, not financial threats. --- ### **3. What You *Can* Do (Without Threats)** Here’s how to respond **from love and wisdom**: 1. **Acknowledge her desire to contribute**: - *"I know you want to help and take care of us. That’s a beautiful heart. Let’s find a way that aligns with God’s plan for us."* 2. **Share your concerns (without judgment)**: - *"I’ve done some research, and most people in these groups lose money. I don’t want you to get stuck paying $1,000 for nothing. What if we tried something else first?"* 3. **Propose alternatives**: - **Side hustles**: "Could we look into a part-time job or skill you could monetize?" - **Joint savings**: "Let’s set aside $100/month together to build an emergency fund." - **Volunteer work**: "What if you used your time to help others in a way that doesn’t cost money?" 4. **Set boundaries (without punishment)**: - If she joins, **agree on consequences in advance**: *"If you go ahead, I’ll need to pause my support for 3 months to see how it goes. If it’s not working, we’ll reassess."* - This is **not a threat—it’s a contract**. It gives her ownership of the decision. 5. **Pray together**: - *"Let’s pray about this. God knows what’s best for us—let’s ask Him to guide us."* --- ### **4. What If She Joins Anyway?** - **Don’t withdraw support immediately**. Give her space to experience the consequences (financial strain, time wasted) without your help. This might be the wake-up call she needs. - **Stay in communication**: Ask how she’s feeling, but don’t enable her. - **Trust God’s timing**: If this is a season of learning, He may use it to teach her about **trusting His provision over human schemes**. --- ### **5. But **love looks like sacrifice, not control**. The best way to "save her" is to **walk alongside her with grace**, not to **push her away with threats**. **Scripture to Meditate On**: > *"Love is patient, love is kind.
